content:Speaker user says: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: What are some ways individuals can support Little Tokyo's cultural institutions and ensure their longevity?

Passage: Campers take a ukulele lesson at the JACCC’s U-Space with Jason Arimoto and Brad Ranola.
Camp Musubi turned 13 this year—a bona fide teenager.
The Japanese American heritage camp’s one-week mission is to connect middle-schoolers to Little Tokyo and the larger Japanese American experience. As families continue moving away from J-Town and Sansei and Yonsei parents don’t have the same ties as our Nisei, making Little Tokyo relevant to the younger generations is more important than ever. Little Tokyo’s history is too rich to forget.
This past July 14-18, we packed five days of camp with 22 presenters and guest speakers, ten workshops, four tours, camp games, one field trip and a whole lot of fun. With camp counselors Mei Yamamoto and Michelle Yamashiro, we planted a lot of seeds. We were gasa gasa, but good gasa gasa.
Four themes emerged from the week and were reinforced at the culminating activity on Friday — a camper-led tour of Little Tokyo for parents and guests.
Hal Keimi from the Little Tokyo Historical Society leads campers on a Little Tokyo tour.
Camp Musubi is dedicated topassing on Little Tokyo’s 130-year history and connecting campers to our pioneering Issei and Nisei. It was a joy watching young people work with our community’s elders this week.
• Priscilla Mui led us through a shibori-dyeing activity that took our T-shirts from humdrum to hi-tone.
• Little Tokyo Historical Society member Hal Keimi led campers on a walking tour and Steve and Patty Nagano shared powerful video from the 1981 Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians hearings.
• Little Tokyo Sustainability Committee member Amy Honjiyo shared the generations-old concept of mottainai and led campers to decorate recycling bins for the Japanese American Cultural and Community Center (JACCC), the site of this year’s camp.
• Community artist Nobuko Miyamoto taught campers American Obon odori songs she’s created: “Mottainai,” “Fandango Obon,” “Yuiyo,” and “Ichigo Ichie.” She explained the meanings of the movements and the lyrics.
• Camp Musubi met San Fernando Valley Japanese American Community Center (SFVJACC) members Nancy Oda, Paul Jonokuchi, and Phil Shigekuni. Campers were given a center tour, treated to a song by seniors in the ukulele class, and exposed to the dedication and work that goes into running a successful center.
The need to document our lives was emphasized by filmmaker Tad Nakamura. He screened his latest film, “Jake Shimabukuro: Life on Four Strings” and talked how the photos we take today will become the archival photos of tomorrow. Tad encouraged campers to capture family gatherings, birthdays and their hobbies and interests.
Campers help serve seniors lunch at the San Fernando Valley Japanese American Community Center.
Learning to give back to the community is part of Camp Musubi’s curriculum. In past years, we’ve pulled weeds at Centenary United Methodist Church, created a Japanese American ABC coloring book for Nishi preschoolers, and played board games with Keiro senior residents.
This year, students donned plastic gloves and hairnets to serve lunch to seniors at the SFVJACC. Camp Musubi, like so many of our community centers, sports leagues and cultural institutions, is volunteer-driven. Providing opportunities to serve the community helps ensure campers are prepared to lead and continue these organizations into the future.
This year campers heard a variety of personal stories that emphasized the importance of finding one’s voice, following your passion and being an ally to others.
Taiko pioneer PJ Hirabayashi from San Jose Taiko talked to campers about being insecure and quiet as a young person until finding her “voice” in drumming. Musicians Jason Arimoto and Brad Ranola from the U-Space at the JACCC shared their love for ukulele through an engaging ukulele lesson.
Sometimes the best way to a student’s mind is through the belly. This year, Kotosh restaurant in Lomita led a sushi-making workshop. Chef Jorge “Koki” Matsumura and camp counselor Michelle Yamashiro have Peruvian and Japanese backgrounds and talked about being proud of their dual identities and how multiple backgrounds can lead to creative fusions of culture — like Kotosh’s California rolls with Peruvian green sauce.
History is a labor of love for historian J.P. De Guzman, who did his doctoral research on the founding of the SFVJACC. This passion came through as he shared his findings with us in a rousing PowerPoint lesson. By teaching campers the unity clap, he emphasized how building community takes teamwork.
Musician and record producer Glenn Suravech talked about his personal journey from Rafu Shimpo reporter, to guitarist for the Asian American indie rock group Visiting Violette, to a recording engineer and producer for Asian American artists. He returned the following day to conduct an impromptu musical jam session with campers and counselors, bringing guitars, drums, and a baritone trumpet. Check out the Camp Musubi Facebook page for video from the ensemble and a classical guitar solo from camper Brandon Wong.
Several other excellent presenters rounded out the week. Keiro Senior HealthCare Community Resource Manager Brandon Leong and intern Ari Sadanaga led a lesson on healthy eating habits, but with a Japanese American twist. Our youngest presenter, 9-year-old Maiya Kuida-Osumi, taught campers how to fold origami paper poppers. Finally, the always supportive Clement Hanami from the Japanese American National Museum gave us a personal tour and activity where campers analyzed artifacts from World War II concentration camps, including a 1943 high school yearbook from Gila River.
This year’s Camp Musubi culminating activity was a camper-led walking tour of Little Tokyo. Each camper was assigned a historic site. It was exciting watching this year’s 13 campers lead parents and guests down historic First Street, tracing the same steps as our pioneering Issei.
Were great-grandparents listening as young people recounted how they boarded buses at First and Central for desert camps? Did generations of Nikkei nod as youth talked about family gatherings at the Far East Cafe? Were newer immigrants taken back as teenagers described the Hiroshima Eternal Peace Flame at Koyasan Buddhist Temple? Were graying Sansei surprised to hear teenagers recall the Little Tokyo Peoples Rights Organization (LTPRO) and late-night noodles at the Atomic Cafe? Did residents overhear campers talk about the teamwork it took to save the San Pedro Firm Building? Did parents’ hearts swell as their children stepped forward as the next caretakers of Little Tokyo history?
Little Tokyo is so much more than just another downtown neighborhood. It’s our sidewalk history book, our family album. If forgotten, we risk losing role models, life lessons, cultural values and our collective memory.
Preserving Little Tokyo’s history is essential to its future as a gathering spot for Japanese Americans. J-Town is an identity anchor for our children in a sea of modern distractions. Getting involved in the community can give them purpose and a 130-year sense of belonging. Take the effort to visit and get involved in Little Tokyo. Along with Camp Musubi, other Little Tokyo youth programs are Project Community, Bridging Community and Rising Stars.
Along with honoring the past, it’s also important to build for the future. There’s fundraising to be done for the Little Tokyo Rec Center/Budokan, support for the JACCC, and we need to understand how the new Metro Regional Connector at First and Central could impact our Japanese American presence in Little Tokyo.
Camp Musubi will be back again next summer. Once again, we’ll be tapping into the power of Little Tokyo, learning with elders, finding our voice, serving the people, having fun, and planting more seeds.
Tony Osumi is Camp Musubi’s Camp Director. He lives in Culver City and teaches third grade at 68th Street Elementary in LAUSD. content:Speaker assistant says: Yes, here are some tips for overcoming the fear of public speaking:

1. Prepare well: Being well-prepared is one of the most effective ways to combat fear. Familiarize yourself with your material and practice your presentation thoroughly.

2. Visualize success: Visualize yourself delivering your speech with confidence and enthusiasm. This will help you feel more comfortable and confident when the time comes.

3. Start with small audiences: Don't start by giving a presentation to a large crowd. Start with smaller audiences and work your way up.

4. Join a public speaking group: Joining a public speaking group can help you practice and gain confidence in a supportive environment.

5. Control your breathing: Take deep breaths and exhale slowly before your presentation. This can help you relax and calm your nerves.

6. Use relaxation techniques: Yoga, meditation, and other relaxation techniques can help you manage anxiety.

7. Focus on the message: Shift your focus from yourself and your fear to the message you want to convey. Think about how your message can help your audience.

8. Get feedback: Ask someone to critique your presentation and give you feedback. This will help you identify areas to improve.

Remember, it's normal to feel nervous about public speaking. It takes time and practice to become comfortable with it, but by following these tips, you can overcome your fear and become a confident public speaker. context:speaker expresses anxiety regarding public speaking, despite utilizing advice for managing nerves, highlighting the desire for immediate relief. keywords: public speaking, fear, confidence, preparation tags: nervousness, public speaking, fear

2. Visualize success: Close your eyes and visualize yourself delivering your presentation with confidence and ease.

3. Stretch and move around: Doing some light movement or stretching can help relieve tension and release endorphins, which can improve your mood.

4. Listen to calming music: Playing some calming music can help you relax and distract you from your nervousness.

5. Repeat affirmations: Repeating positive affirmations such as "I am confident and capable" can help you feel more self-assured.

6. Avoid caffeine and sugar: Caffeine and sugar can make you feel jittery and anxious, so it's best to avoid them before your presentation.

The theater, which was nearly demolished in the 1980s in favor of a parking lot, was renovated and re-opened in 2006 thanks to a partnership between the foundation and the City of El Paso. Also being screened on Sunday afternoon were a sold-out showing of the film "Selena," the biopic about the beloved fallen Tejano singer starring Jennifer Lopez, and the Audrey Hepburn musical "Funny Face." Closing out the fest Sunday night was the classic British comedy "Monty Python and the Holy Grail," which is celebrating its 40th anniversary. "My parents used to come and drop us off here when we were kids," East El Pasoan Manny Martinez said. "We would buy 10-cent hot dogs — my cousin, myself and my brother. That's part of the fun of coming to the festival, I make it a point to come every year, at least to a couple of showings." This year, the festival, which regularly brings in celebrity guests to talk about the classic films in which they starred, included appearances by actress Louise Fletcher and Cindy Williams. Fletcher won an Academy Award for her portrayal of Nurse Ratched in the 1975 film "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest." Williams, best known for her role as Shirley Feeney in the hit television show "Laverne & Shirley" in the 1970s and '80s, appeared at a screening of George Lucas' first hit film "American Graffiti" on Friday. "Cindy Williams is a sweetheart," Doug Pullen, the festival's creative director, said. "We had a private reception for her before (her appearance). When we walked her over to the theater for the red carpet and the line was outside all the way around the building. Before I knew it she was greeting people and taking pictures with them. She had a cold the whole time so instead of hugging and shaking hands she was rubbing elbows with people. And Fletcher was great too." One of the festival's best attended events was the Aug. 8 free outdoor screening of the campy musical "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," Pullen said. He estimated more than 4,000 film-lovers enjoyed the cult classic whose fans enjoy dressing up as its characters, acting out the film as it plays and various other traditions such as throwing toast and rice at various points in the movie. The 1939 epic Civil War romance "Gone With the Wind" and the 1985 time travel adventure "Back to the Future," were both equally well attended, attracting about 1,600 people each, Pullen said. "I think it's great that we have people interested in seeing films spanning 46 years," Pullen said. Another annual tradition which has kept people coming to the festival year after year is the theater's light show, which illuminates the ceiling in a night sky scene, and the Mighty Wurlitzer Organ, played on the final day by Ken Fedorick and several other volunteers throughout the festival. "I love the theater," West El Pasoan Debbie Hinshaw said. "I love when they show the stars and the organ. I like that it's very diverse and that they have things for all age groups and different interests." Something new at the Plaza Classic this year was the addition of a two-week kids camp. Campers were taught filmmaking basics and made short films which were screened, along with other local shorts and features, in the El Paso Community Foundation's Foundation Room, located just around the corner from the Plaza on Oregon Street. The camp had 18 participants and Pullen said it will return for next year's festival. The Local Flavor series, featuring local filmmakers, has also continued to grow, Pullen said. Some of the screenings played to a capacity audience, he said. "Last year we tripled the previous year's attendance (for Local Flavor) and we can safely say we had a higher attendance this year," Pullen said. Part of what makes the festival possible each year is the work of many volunteers who take tickets, usher people to their seats and answer questions for festival-goers. Luis Suira is a second-year volunteer. He decided to volunteer because he liked the festival and the theater it calls home. "I think bringing classic films to El Paso is a great way to bring the community together in a truly fantastic place," Suira said. "I've seen some people that genuinely didn't realize that the Plaza was still (around). People come in and you see the amazement in their eyes. They look around the main hall and see the huge ceilings, the colors, the bar — its really nice to see." Organizing the festival is a year round affair, Pullen said. He's already making mental notes for next year's Plaza Classic, which is set for Aug. 4-14, and the festival's tenth anniversary in two years. While no concrete plans are in place yet, other than the dates, he hopes to continue the Plaza Classic's partnerships with the El Paso Chihuahuas and with the El Paso museums of art and history. The baseball movie "The Natural," starring Robert Redford kicked off the festival two weeks ago at Southwest University Park and the two Downtown museums hosted events and exhibits around the screenings of "Gone With the Wind" and several of pop artist Andy Warhol's films. "We're already getting requests to show "Back to the Future (Part II)," Pullen said. "People have asked me for more sci-fi and horror. content:Speaker assistant says: 1. Pack Healthy Snacks:
When on a long road trip, it is common to munch on unhealthy snacks like chips, cookies, and chocolates. To avoid this, pack healthy snacks like fruits, raw veggies, and nuts. These foods have essential nutrients that help keep you full and provide energy. Also, you can pack protein bars or protein shakes to provide you with extra energy.

2. Take Breaks to Exercise:
Long hours on the road can take a toll on your body, and sitting for an extended period can cause stiffness, cramps, and other issues. Take frequent breaks to stretch your body and do some light exercise. Stop at a nearby park or rest area to do some simple exercises like jumping jacks, squats, and lunges. If you have access to a gym near your road, it's a perfect opportunity to go there and work out.

3. Plan Your Meals Ahead of Time:
Eating healthy on the road can be challenging, but with a bit of planning, it's possible. Before hitting the road, plan your meals ahead of time. You can look for restaurants or cafes that have healthy meal options or pack pre-made meals like salads, sandwiches, and wraps. If you can invest in a cooler, pack it with healthy foods like yogurt, boiled eggs, cheese, and veggies. This way, you will have healthy food options, and you won't succumb to fast food and other unhealthy options along the way.

Bonus tip: Stay hydrated
Drinking enough water is essential, especially during long trips. Dehydration can make you feel sluggish and tired. Make sure to pack enough water bottles, or stop at rest areas to refuel. content:Speaker assistant says: Introduction

Sustainability is becoming increasingly relevant in daily life, with more and more people recognizing the importance of environmentally responsible living. While it may seem challenging for city dwellers to lead a sustainable lifestyle, there are many easy steps that can be taken to make a positive impact. This guide is designed to provide practical tips for reducing your environmental footprint and living a more sustainable life in the city.

Chapter 1: Reducing Waste

Waste reduction is an essential aspect of sustainable living. Here are some simple steps you can take towards reducing waste in the city:

1. Use reusable bags for shopping and avoid single-use plastic bags.

2. Carry a reusable water bottle and coffee cup instead of purchasing disposable ones.

3. Compost- set up a container on your balcony or use the community garden compost bin.

4. Switch to reusable containers instead of single-use plastics.

5. Say no to paper vouchers and receipts.

6. Recycle- make sure you recycle waste properly and frequently.

Chapter 2: Green Energy Alternatives

Using renewable and green energy sources are crucial steps in reducing your carbon footprint. Here are some ways you can switch to green energy alternatives:

1. Install solar panels-take advantage of government solar energy incentives and install solar panels on your roof.

2. Use energy-efficient light bulbs and appliances

3. Use natural light instead of artificial lighting.

4. Invest in green energy – consider a green electricity supplier to reduce your greenhouse gas emissions.

Chapter 3: Sustainable Transportation

Transportation is a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions. As a city dweller, here are some tips that you can adopt to lead a sustainable transportation lifestyle.

1. Bicycle, walking or use public transport- avoid car trips for shorter distances.

2. Carpool- share rides with friends and colleagues.

3. Use electric vehicles- use an electric car, bike or scooter.

Chapter 4: Eco-Friendly Consumer Choices

Consumers have the power to make a change through environmentally responsible product choices. Here are some tips to minimize your impact through consumer choices:

1. Purchase second-hand goods- check out flea markets, garage sales or thrift stores. Avoid fast fashion and overconsumption.

2. Choose eco-friendly, plant-based cleaning products.

3. Be selective about packaging- choose products with minimal packaging, or with eco-friendly packaging made from recycled materials.

Chapter 5: Local Food Sourcing

Consuming local food options is not only good for the environment but also supports the local economy. Here's how you can consume more local food in the city:

1. Join a community-led farm share.

To reduce the impact of air travel on greenhouse gas emissions, several measures can be taken, including:

1. Improved aircraft design: Manufacturers can design more fuel-efficient aircraft and engines that consume less fuel and emit fewer pollutants.

2. Use biofuels: The aviation industry can switch to sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) made from biofuels such as algae or waste biomass. These fuels emit fewer greenhouse gases and other pollutants than traditional jet fuels.

3. Carbon offsetting: Airlines can invest in carbon offset programs, which reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions from other sources to balance the emissions produced by their flights.

4. Flight optimization: Pilots and air traffic controllers can work together to optimize flight paths, speeds, and altitudes to reduce fuel consumption and emissions.

5. Encourage alternative modes of transportation: Governments can invest in high-speed rail, which is less polluting than air travel, and encourage people to travel by rail or electric vehicles for short distances.

6. Reduce air travel demand: Individuals can reduce their air travel by opting for virtual meetings or choosing to travel by alternative modes of transportation.

By implementing these measures, the aviation industry can significantly reduce its greenhouse gas emissions and contribute to the fight against climate change. context:Passengers can minimize the environmental impact of air travel by choosing direct flights, opting for economy class, packing light, selecting sustainable airlines, utilizing carbon offsetting programs, and reducing travel frequency. keywords: air travel, greenhouse gas emissions, aviation, carbon emissions tags: greenhouse gas emissions, carbon offsetting

content:Speaker assistant says: As passengers, there are several things we can do to reduce the impact of air travel on the environment. Here are some tips:

1. Choose direct flights: Direct flights produce fewer emissions than flights with layovers since takeoffs and landings represent the most significant source of emissions.

2. Fly economy class: Flying business or first class takes up more space, resulting in a higher carbon footprint per passenger. Opting for economy class is an easy way to reduce your carbon footprint.

3. Pack light: The more baggage a plane carries, the more fuel it burns. Packing lightly and only bringing what is necessary can help reduce the weight of the plane and, therefore, reduce emissions.

4. Choose airlines with sustainable practices: When booking your flights, consider airlines that are implementing measures to reduce their carbon footprint, such as using sustainable aviation fuels.

5. Use carbon offsetting: Many airlines offer the option to offset the carbon emissions produced by your flight by investing in projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions from the atmosphere.

6. Travel less frequently: Consider alternative modes of transportation for shorter distances or reducing the number of times you fly. You can also consider virtual meetings instead of traveling to meetings when possible.

These are a few ways individuals can reduce the impact of air travel on the environment when they have to fly. content:Speaker assistant says: Airlines can adjust their flight schedules during peak seasons to accommodate more passengers, but they are often limited by airport capacity and aircraft availability. During peak seasons, airlines prioritize routes that have high demand and increase the frequency of flights. However, airport capacity limits how many flights an airport can handle in a given period. This is because airports have specific runways, gates, and other infrastructure that can only handle a certain number of planes at a given time. 

In addition, airlines are also limited by the availability of aircraft. Increasing the frequency of flights requires more planes, and if an airline doesn't have enough aircraft available, they won't be able to add more flights. 

Despite these limitations, airlines can make adjustments to their flight schedules to accommodate more passengers during peak season. They can lease aircraft from other airlines, use larger planes or shift flights to less busy times of the day. A busy airport with limited capacity can also lead to delays and cancellations, which is why airlines try to adjust schedules with enough time to minimize the impact on passengers. 2. Pack smart: Use packing cubes or compression bags to maximize space and keep your items organized.

3. Consider the airline's baggage allowance: Check the airline's baggage guidelines and restrictions before you pack.

4. Plan outfits ahead of time: Planning what you'll wear during your trip can help you avoid overpacking and save time getting ready.

5. Pack essentials in your carry-on: Pack items such as your passport, medication, and valuables in your carry-on bag to ensure they're safe and easily accessible.

content:Speaker assistant says: There are several ways to get from the airport to your hotel in Bangkok:

1. Taxi: Taxis are available outside the arrival terminals at both Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang airports. The fare should cost around 300-500 THB depending on the distance and traffic.

2. Airport Rail Link: The Airport Rail Link connects both airports to downtown Bangkok. Take the train to the station closest to your hotel and then a taxi or other mode of transportation from there.

3. Airport Shuttle Bus: Some hotels offer airport shuttle buses to and from the airport. Check with your hotel to see if this service is available.

4. Private Car: You can also arrange a private car transfer in advance.
